title: Offerings
hookLine: a birthday, eleven dollars, and a poet who gives away forests and lakes he doesn't own
tomorrow: when Shantideva gets scared, where does he run?

lines: THE CHEAP STUFF FEELS LIKE AN APOLOGY.
HE HAD NOTHING IN HIS HANDS.
cards: A birthday is coming for someone you love, and your bank app says eleven dollars. You scroll gift guides anyway. Everything worth giving seems to cost more than you have, and the cheap stuff feels like an apology.
So you start to wonder whether you should just send a card and say nothing. Shantideva stood exactly there, with nothing in his hands, wanting to give the best he could imagine.
What he did next is the strangest gift list ever written.

teach.h: I HAVE NOTHING ELSE TO GIVE.
teach.b: Chapter two opens with offerings to the Buddhas, the teaching and the bodhisattvas. And then a confession in the middle of it: I have no merit, I'm poor, I have nothing else to give. So he offers what nobody owns.
Flowers and fruit. Healing herbs. Clear, cool water.
Mountains, and quiet forests where trees bend with blossoms.
Lakes covered in lotuses, with the cry of wild geese. Crops growing in the fields. All of it, as far as space goes, belonging to no one.
Here's the move that makes it work.

teach.h: AN OFFERING IS NOT A PAYMENT.
teach.b: Offering, in Buddhist practice, isn't a payment. A flower on an altar doesn't buy anything. It's a way of turning toward what you love and saying: this, for you.
So a lake you'll never own can still be given, because the giving is in the turning.
And then he goes one step further, and offers himself: his whole body and life, to the Buddhas and their children, to use as they will. The person with eleven dollars has more than they think.
The light on the street at six o'clock. A walk to the place they love. Your full attention for an afternoon.

how: Buddhists often set out flowers, water, light and incense at a shrine as offerings, and some Tibetan practices offer the whole world in the imagination, as Shantideva does in this chapter.

games.q: your best friend just got bad news and you're broke until payday. what would Shantideva's list suggest?
o: wait until payday so you can get her something real.
bring her somewhere beautiful that's free, and give her your whole attention.
send a long apology for not having anything to give.
games.why: Shantideva's offering starts from empty hands. a place nobody owns and your full attention can still be given.

practice: Look out the nearest window, or at the sky, or at one plant in the room. Choose one beautiful thing in sight that belongs to no one.
Rest your eyes on it for the whole sit, and in your own words, silently, give it to someone you love.

wordCard.voice: Offerings: what Shantideva gives when his hands are empty. Forests, lakes and fields that no one owns, and finally himself.

orig.note: Sanskrit: worship, honoring, offering. Chapter two opens with Shantideva's offerings to the Buddhas.

carryVoice: Your line: offer the unowned. The sky was never for sale, and it can still be a gift. Chapter two, begun.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 2.1-2.8 (offerings; 'I have nothing else to give'; everything unowned; the offering of oneself)
